note.explanation: Metals and non-metals have different physical properties. Metals are usually strong, shiny, and good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals are usually brittle and poor conductors. Graphite conducts electricity, and iodine is lustrous, so these are exceptions.
examples: Copper is a metal: it is lustrous and conducts electricity.
Sulphur is a non-metal: it is brittle and does not conduct electricity.
note.checkAnswer: Metals are usually good conductors; non-metals are usually poor conductors. Graphite is an exception.
note.simple: Metals are usually strong and conduct heat and electricity. Non-metals usually break easily and do not conduct them.

note.title: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
steps: Metals can be hammered into thin sheets; this property is called malleability.
Metals can be drawn into wires; this property is called ductility.
Non-metals are generally brittle, so they break when hammered or stretched.
Graphite is the exception among non-metals because it conducts electricity.

written.text: Why are almost all the metals solids while non-metals generally exist as gases and solids?
written.finalAnswer: Strong metallic bonds give metals high melting points, so almost all are solids at room temperature. Non-metals have weaker bonds and a wider range of melting points, so they generally occur as gases or solids at room temperature.

written.text: Why are metals generally tough and strong whereas non-metals are neither tough nor strong?
written.finalAnswer: Metals are generally tough and strong because their atoms are held together by strong metallic bonds. Non-metals are neither tough nor strong because their bonds are weak and they are non-ductile and non-malleable; they break easily.

written.text: Compare the properties of metals and non-metals.
written.finalAnswer: Metals generally have high melting and boiling points, conduct heat and electricity well, and are malleable, ductile, lustrous, tough, and strong. Non-metals may be solids, liquids, or gases at room temperature; they have a wide range of melting and boiling points, are generally poor conductors, brittle, dull, and neither tough nor strong. Graphite conducts electricity, iodine is lustrous, and mercury is a liquid metal.

examTips: A comparison question may ask for several physical properties of metals and non-metals. Use paired points so the examiner can see both sides clearly.
For a reason question about strength, connect the properties to bonding: metals have strong metallic bonds, while non-metals have weak bonds and are brittle.
Name exceptions when they are relevant: graphite conducts electricity, iodine is lustrous, mercury is not a solid, and graphite and diamond have high melting points.
Use the correct terms: malleability means forming sheets, and ductility means drawing into wires.

example.question: Compare the properties of metals and non-metals.
example.answer: Metals are generally good conductors, malleable, ductile, lustrous, tough, strong, and have high melting and boiling points. Non-metals are generally poor conductors, brittle, dull, and neither tough nor strong, and have a wide range of melting and boiling points. Graphite conducts electricity, iodine is lustrous, and mercury is a liquid metal.

explain.title: Metals can be shaped
explain.body: Metals can be hammered into thin sheets. This property is called malleability. Metals can also be drawn into wires; this property is called ductility.

explain.title: Metals conduct and shine
explain.body: Metallic bonding allows metals to conduct heat and electricity well. Metals are usually lustrous, which means they have a shiny appearance.

explain.title: Non-metals are usually brittle
explain.body: Non-metals cannot generally be hammered into sheets or drawn into wires. They break because they are brittle and their bonds are weak.

explain.title: Remember the exceptions
explain.body: Graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity. Iodine is an exception to the usual dull appearance of non-metals. Mercury is an exception to metals being solids, and graphite and diamond are exceptions to non-metals having low melting points.

mistakes: Do not swap the meanings of malleability and ductility: sheets are malleability; wires are ductility.
Do not write that all non-metals are gases; they can be solids, liquids, or gases at room temperature.
Do not say non-metals never conduct electricity: graphite is an exception.
Do not forget exceptions when a question asks for a comparison: mercury, iodine, graphite, and diamond matter in this section.
Do not explain the strength of metals by saying they are simply hard; connect the explanation to strong metallic bonds.
